selection: Thirty researched cases selected for organizational need, role fit and advanced-level evidence. Grouped by pathway, not ranked by debut probability; no league-rank cutoff.

coverage.pitchLevelMeasurements: Not independently collected. Specific weaknesses are attributed to dated scouting reports; proposed monitors are not claimed as measurements.

players.name: Ryan Sloan
players.why: His Double-A work makes a direct jump worth watching. Seattle already has six pitchers who made multiple MLB starts; a vacancy or a need for an extra starter is the realistic entry point.
players.opportunity: An injury, workload break or rotation change could create starts. Beating the next depth option matters more than his prospect rank; a full-time rotation place is not currently open.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports a glove-side location bias and a less consistent slider than splitter.
players.checkpoint: Command fastballs to the arm side, repeat the slider’s shape, and hold pitch quality deeper into starts.
players.monitor: Track arm-side target execution, slider consistency and late-start velocity; those pitch-level measurements have not been collected here.
players.need: Rotation coverage, not an unfilled everyday role. Six current options started MLB games, so opportunity depends on health, workload and depth ordering.
players.organization: Yoho and a Bottle of Rum
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Liam Doyle
players.why: A full Double-A starting workload gives him a route beyond his ranking. St. Louis used Pallante, Leahy, Liberatore and McGreevy for at least 29 starts each, with Mathews and Dobbins also starting.
players.opportunity: He must displace a rotation option or answer an injury need. A shorter bullpen assignment is another possible debut route, but would not mean he has passed the starter test.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes an overpowering fastball, but a slower breaker that can show early and draws little chase. Its report calls for a breaking-ball adjustment.
players.checkpoint: Make the breaker less recognizable out of the hand, command secondaries for strikes, and reduce walks while retaining a starter’s workload.
players.monitor: Follow breaking-ball chase and strike rates separately. The saved 2026 walk rate is a warning, not proof that a specific grip fix will work.
players.need: Potential rotation competition rather than a guaranteed vacancy. The incumbent group has a full season of starts; pitch execution must justify displacing someone.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Jamie Arnold
players.why: His season workload supports a starting path, but five Triple-A innings are only a brief introduction. The stronger question is whether his fastball control holds against advanced hitters.
players.need: Several listed starters posted ERAs above 5.00, including Springs, Lopez, Perkins and Jump. That creates performance pressure rather than a promised vacancy.
players.opportunity: Outperform the next rotation option, with a depth assignment possible first. Other young pitchers also compete for the same innings.
players.observed: FanGraphs’ April report describes poor fastball strike/zone rates and falling behind, forcing heavy slider use to recover counts.
players.checkpoint: Get fastball strikes earlier in counts and command a complementary pitch so the slider is not always a rescue pitch.
players.monitor: Follow fastball strike rate and counts won early; the five-inning Triple-A ERA is not proof that the control problem is solved.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Carlos Lagrange
players.why: His Triple-A experience puts him close enough for a depth call, but New York already has a substantial rotation group. The first MLB role could be shorter than the eventual development goal.
players.need: The established starters mostly performed well; this is more about injury coverage or bullpen usefulness than an obvious starting-rotation production hole.
players.opportunity: Compete for depth innings or earn a relief assignment with a repeatable strike-throwing case. A fastball reaching triple digits does not create an automatic rotation slot.
players.observed: FanGraphs highlights elite velocity and multiple secondary options, but delivery effort and walks make relief a plausible outcome.
players.checkpoint: Repeat release timing and reduce free passes while retaining fastball quality and a dependable secondary strike.
players.monitor: Separate shorter-stint effectiveness from starter command; a relief debut would not mean the rotation questions were answered.
players.organization: Yoho and a Bottle of Rum
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Jack Wenninger
players.role: Rotation depth with a developed workload
players.why: A full Triple-A workload makes him a practical depth candidate even far outside the league’s top 100. His 2026 walks also show why an earlier positive report is not the same as present readiness.
players.need: Manaea posted a 4.78 ERA and Senga 7.34, while McLean, Scott and Thornton supply competition. Better depth has a plausible use.
players.opportunity: Win a spot-start or next-man-up assignment, then show he can hold it. The trade-value ranking does not decide the MLB depth ordering.
players.observed: FanGraphs sees a useful splitter and developed workload, but says too many breaking balls are flat, soft or backed up.
players.checkpoint: Make the breaker’s quality repeatable and restore better strike throwing, rather than leaning only on the splitter.
players.monitor: Track breaker execution and free passes; distinguish last season’s favorable control report from the higher saved 2026 walk rate.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Andrew Fischer
players.why: Third base is a more plausible route than first base: Milwaukee split third-base work among Hamilton, Ortiz and Vaughn. Fischer’s Double-A power puts him in that conversation despite a much lower league ranking.
players.opportunity: He has to win third-base work, not inherit an empty job. Moving to first or DH adds competition from Bauers, Vaughn, Yelich, Adams and Burke.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports swings over changeups, including pitches inside the zone, and hesitation on slow rollers.
players.checkpoint: Improve in-zone contact against changeups; make cleaner decisions on slow rollers at third.
players.monitor: Separate changeup contact from overall strikeouts. His Double-A strikeout rate is context, not a measured changeup-whiff rate.
players.need: A possible offensive upgrade at third: Hamilton posted a .650 OPS and Ortiz .730. Their defense still matters, and Fischer must earn the position.
players.organization: Yoho and a Bottle of Rum
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Luke Adams
players.why: His Triple-A sample and balanced strikeout/walk counts deserve attention even outside the top 100. First base is crowded; showing usable third-base defense would give him another way onto the roster.
players.opportunity: Vaughn already provides a right-handed first-base option. Adams needs an injury, transaction or a better all-around case; he and Burke cannot both be credited with the same hypothetical opening.
players.observed: FanGraphs questions whether modest contact impact and a walk/HBP-heavy approach clear the offensive bar at first base.
players.checkpoint: Turn hittable strikes into harder contact; preserve enough third-base defense to offer another route.
players.monitor: Watch damage on strikes and performance at third, rather than treating every walk or hit-by-pitch as proof of MLB readiness.
players.need: No obvious first-base production hole: Vaughn posted an .834 OPS and Bauers .873. Versatility or an offseason change is the stronger route.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Jesus Made
players.why: A substantial Double-A sample makes skipping Triple-A plausible. But Turang’s second-base workload and Pratt/Ortiz at short mean that elite prospect status does not create an automatic middle-infield vacancy.
players.opportunity: Third base or an infield reshuffle could open a route if he is defensively ready. That also puts him in competition with Fischer, rather than giving each a separate open position.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports 81% in-zone contact in 2025, alongside inconsistent accuracy on routine throws.
players.checkpoint: Clean up routine throws and footwork; maintain in-zone contact as the pitching improves.
players.monitor: Review routine-play execution and advanced-level contact. The 81% figure is historical scouting data, not a fresh 2026 Prospect Savant measurement.
players.need: Third-base competition is more plausible than a second-base opening: Turang played 151 games there with an .816 OPS. A shortstop route also has competition.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Sebastian Walcott
players.why: The bat returned strongly after an interrupted season, but the highest-level sample is tiny. Texas has Seager at short, Jung at third and established outfield/DH options; health and defensive fit matter more than the ranking.
players.opportunity: An injury or roster change could create a bat-first route. Outfield work is a possible alternative, not evidence that Texas has promised him an outfield job.
players.observed: FanGraphs’ October report describes his February elbow surgery, July return, mostly DH usage and resumed infield work plus reported outfield drills in the Fall League.
players.checkpoint: Demonstrate healthy, repeatable throws and usable defense at an available position; sustain the bat over a larger advanced-level sample.
players.monitor: Watch defensive workload and throwing recovery. This report does not justify labeling him weak against elevated fastballs.
players.need: No obvious infield vacancy: Seager remains the shortstop and Jung produced an .827 OPS. A healthy bat plus defensive flexibility creates more options.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Leo De Vries
players.why: His advanced-level record earns a debut watch. Wilson occupies shortstop; Gelof, Muncy, McNeil and Kuroda-Grauer already have work at second or third, so moving off short does not make the competition disappear.
players.opportunity: A third-base opportunity or infield reshuffle is more plausible than assuming he immediately replaces Wilson. He still needs to win that role with both the bat and glove.
players.observed: FanGraphs sees broad offensive potential but inconsistent accuracy on deeper shortstop throws, and identifies third base as a possible alternative behind Wilson.
players.checkpoint: Improve accuracy on long throws and demonstrate reliable defense at the position that actually opens.
players.monitor: Compare throwing consistency and position-specific reps alongside advanced-level contact and power. A positional switch remains conditional.
players.need: Third base is worth testing: Muncy posted a .683 OPS, while Wilson holds shortstop. Gelof’s .797 OPS and cross-position usage complicate that route.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Caleb Bonemer
players.why: Double-A power makes him relevant, but Chicago’s infield is occupied: Vargas at third, Montgomery at short, Meidroth at second and Murakami at first. Antonacci also logged substantial left-field work.
players.opportunity: He needs to beat an incumbent, learn a usable alternative position or benefit from a roster change. Being a top prospect alone does not make this a clear 2027 starting job.
players.observed: FanGraphs identifies fastballs up and away, related changeup vulnerability and inconsistent throws as development areas; second base or left field are possible alternatives.
players.checkpoint: Improve contact against upper-away fastballs without selling out against changeups; make reliable throws at his eventual position.
players.monitor: Track those pitch/location groups separately and watch defensive assignments. Overall home-run totals cannot answer either question.
players.need: Third base is not an offensive need: Vargas posted an .837 OPS across 704 PA. A move there alone would not remove the blocker.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Charlie Condon
players.why: A full Triple-A season gives him a stronger proximity case than a brief promotion alone. The right-field/corner mix offers a more plausible route than assuming first base is available.
players.need: Beck posted a .552 OPS, while Johnston and Moniak also took corner work. Rumfield’s .843 OPS makes first base a less obvious production hole.
players.opportunity: Win a corner-outfield share with the bat and playable defense. The Triple-A environment can inflate offense, so raw slugging is not a direct MLB forecast.
players.observed: FanGraphs identifies a rigid bat path and trouble recognizing spin despite substantial raw power; its report also notes prior hand/wrist injuries.
players.checkpoint: Recognize breaking balls earlier and keep contact quality against spin while showing a healthy, repeatable swing.
players.monitor: Compare breaking-ball chase/contact and production away from hitter-friendly parks; no fresh pitch-type split is claimed here.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Ralphy Velazquez
players.why: A substantial Triple-A sample and power production give him a route beyond prospect status. Cleveland already has several first-base options, so he must improve that group rather than simply reach the level.
players.need: Manzardo posted a .684 OPS, Lowe .651 and Hoskins .682. That suggests an offensive upgrade opportunity, although it does not remove roster and defensive competition.
players.opportunity: Earn first-base work with the bat; viable corner-outfield defense would add flexibility. DeLauter and Kwan make an outfield starting spot less automatic.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes a sound contact/power foundation at first base; corner-outfield routes and positioning still need work because speed limits the margin for error.
players.checkpoint: Maintain selective two-strike contact against advanced pitching and become reliable enough in a corner to offer a second position.
players.monitor: Track advanced-level contact plus outfield reads and routes; there is no sourced reason here to invent a specific high-fastball weakness.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Franklin Arias
players.why: His Triple-A sample and low strikeout rate support a genuine readiness watch. Shortstop defense is part of the case, unlike a bat-only prospect needing an immediate power breakthrough.
players.need: Story posted a .622 OPS and Monasterio .666. An offensive upgrade is possible, but roster decisions and incumbents’ defense still determine access.
players.opportunity: Compete at short or demonstrate useful second-base flexibility. Durbin already logged 151 games at third; moving around the infield is not the same as finding an empty job.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports elite contact and polished shortstop defense, with room for added strength/power and better handling of hard-hit grounders.
players.checkpoint: Preserve contact as velocity rises, turn added strength into game damage and handle sharply hit grounders cleanly.
players.monitor: Track contact and damage together at the higher level; do not manufacture a whiff problem in a player whose reported strength is contact.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Theo Gillen
players.why: His Double-A contact/power record makes an accelerated path possible. Whether he can play center matters because it gives Tampa Bay another way to fit the bat.
players.need: Mullins posted a .628 OPS in substantial center-field work; Simpson already took most left-field games, while DeLuca and Mesa also fill the outfield mix.
players.opportunity: Win center-field confidence or out-hit a corner option. A move to left would create more direct competition with Simpson, rather than solve every roster question.
players.observed: FanGraphs links some misses to a high-effort swing and moving head, and describes center-field defense as still developing after an infield-to-outfield conversion.
players.checkpoint: Keep the head steadier through contact and improve center-field reads/routes without losing the power gains.
players.monitor: Monitor in-zone contact alongside center-field positioning; the report does not identify a specific pitch type as the sole problem.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Nelson Rada
players.why: A full Triple-A season and a center-field skill set provide a debut route without needing top-100 status. His current offensive shape fits a reserve role more easily than an instant middle-order job.
players.need: Lowe posted a .633 OPS, while Trout handled 109 center-field games and Siri provides competition. Defensive coverage could matter even without a full-time opening.
players.opportunity: Earn a fourth-outfielder assignment or cover a center-field absence. Regular playing time requires the bat to contribute enough alongside the glove.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes plus center-field defense and an advanced approach, but very limited power and too many caught-stealing outs in the prior season.
players.checkpoint: Improve stolen-base decisions and retain quality contact against advanced velocity; more steals alone are not proof of better baserunning.
players.monitor: Track caught-stealing efficiency and contact quality, not only stolen-base totals or batting average.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Max Anderson
players.why: His substantial Triple-A contact record makes a bench-bat route worth examining despite a low league rank. Detroit’s multiple infield options make versatility more useful than a single-position label.
players.need: McGonigle already supplies strong infield production and Torres, Lee and Keith have substantial usage. McKinstry’s .582 OPS suggests a possible bench upgrade, not an open starting job.
players.opportunity: Beat a utility option or establish a role against left-handers while covering second and third. Playing time would depend on matchups and defensive trust.
players.observed: FanGraphs identifies an aggressive approach and a late load that can lose to good velocity or hard spin; limited range narrows the defensive fit.
players.checkpoint: Get the load started on time against firm pitching and avoid chasing pitches he cannot drive.
players.monitor: Compare fastball timing, chase and results by pitcher handedness rather than assuming the Triple-A average fully translates.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Parks Harber
players.why: A meaningful Triple-A sample makes him a plausible depth option. His production there is less forceful than the combined season line, so earning a role still requires an offensive adjustment.
players.need: Chapman posted a .692 OPS, but Schmitt also covers third. Devers and Eldridge already provide strong first-base/DH offense, limiting a bat-only fallback.
players.opportunity: Show reliable third-base cover and a bat useful enough to carry on the bench. A first-base move does not create a clear vacancy.
players.observed: FanGraphs flags early hip opening that may expose spin down and away, with elevated elite velocity another test; third-base play is reliable but range-limited.
players.checkpoint: Stay through the outer half against breaking balls and demonstrate enough timely contact against premium fastballs.
players.monitor: Track those pitch/location groups and third-base reliability; his higher-level decline should not be hidden inside all-level totals.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: James Tibbs III
players.why: A full Triple-A workload and substantial power give him a practical depth case beyond his league rank. The Dodgers’ roster, rather than a need for more minor-league home runs, is the main access question.
players.need: The corner, first-base and DH roles are already heavily occupied; De Paula has also debuted. There is no clean everyday vacancy in this snapshot.
players.opportunity: Earn a corner/first-base reserve or matchup assignment after a roster change. He and Sirota are competing for overlapping depth opportunities, not separate guaranteed openings.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes sound swing decisions but only fair corner defense, occasional vulnerability to velocity and limited power against elite left-handers.
players.checkpoint: Handle premium velocity and produce more damage against left-handers while staying reliable at both corner positions.
players.monitor: Measure left-on-left damage separately from contact; good overall walks do not establish an everyday role.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Enrique Bradfield Jr.
players.why: Triple-A experience plus a defense/speed role gives him a path independent of top-prospect status. A reserve debut could be useful to Baltimore before the bat is ready for everyday work.
players.need: Taveras posted a .633 OPS and Cowser .687, while both played center. The relevant need could be defensive coverage or a better bench mix rather than a vacant starting position.
players.opportunity: Win a fourth-outfielder or pinch-running assignment and show enough offense to keep it. That kind of debut need not bring regular fantasy at-bats.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes strong contact decisions and center-field defense, but weak damage on softer pitches and difficulty lifting pitches in the lower third.
players.checkpoint: Create more useful contact on low strikes without losing contact or expanding the strike zone.
players.monitor: Track low-zone damage and power/contact trade-offs; verify health after the older report’s hand-discomfort note.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Blake Burke
players.why: He reached Triple-A, so he belongs in the discussion beyond the highly ranked names. But his Triple-A production fell sharply from Double-A; the combined season line hides that adjustment.
players.opportunity: Bauers already fills the left-handed first-base role and Yelich gets DH work. Burke needs better Triple-A results plus an opening, while also competing with Adams and Fischer.
players.observed: FanGraphs frames elite elevated fastballs and MLB left-handers as unresolved tests, not established failures.
players.checkpoint: Prove he can catch high-end velocity upstairs and remain competitive against left-handers.
players.monitor: Track upper-zone fastball contact and left-on-left results with sample sizes. Do not infer either split from the aggregate strikeout rate.
players.need: A left-handed first-base bat is already supplied by Bauers, who posted an .873 OPS. Burke needs to improve before claiming a meaningful upgrade.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Alfredo Duno
players.why: Double-A experience gives his bat a plausible accelerated path, but Stephenson and Trevino already handle catching. First base is not an easy shortcut with Stewart and Steer also there.
players.opportunity: A catching vacancy helps only if Cincinnati trusts his receiving. A bat-only promotion would require a separate lineup opening; a debut need not bring regular catching at-bats.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports 69% contact in 2025, with elevated fastballs causing most misses, and receiving that still needs refinement.
players.checkpoint: Increase contact on elevated fastballs while improving pitch receiving and sustaining the catching workload.
players.monitor: Separate fastball contact and receiving progress. The historical contact figure is not a current-season whiff measurement.
players.need: Backup-catching offense could improve on Trevino’s .557 OPS, but that role requires receiving trust and would offer limited starts behind Stephenson.
players.organization: Yoho and a Bottle of Rum
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Mike Sirota
players.why: His saved Triple-A sample is only nine PA, so the highest-level label is not proof of readiness. Los Angeles has Pages in center and established corner bats; De Paula has already debuted and Ohtani occupies most DH opportunities.
players.opportunity: A center-field-capable reserve offers more paths than a corner-only bat. He must demonstrate that defense and out-hit other depth options; a crowded roster makes an everyday debut less straightforward.
players.observed: FanGraphs’ 2025 report pairs a 53% hard-hit rate with below-average in-zone contact, mistimed swings underneath fastballs and imperfect center-field routes.
players.checkpoint: Improve in-zone fastball contact and center-field reads while retaining impact on contact.
players.monitor: Compare fastball contact and defensive routes at the higher level. The 53% hard-hit figure comes from the older, injury-shortened sample.
players.need: A flexible outfield reserve is a more realistic need than an instant starting job: Pages logged 132 center-field games with an .811 OPS.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Rainiel Rodriguez
players.why: His Double-A exposure is encouraging for his age, but St. Louis already used Herrera, Pagés, Crooks and Bernal behind the plate. His ceiling is not evidence of an immediate catching vacancy.
players.opportunity: He needs defensive trust and a place in the catching rotation. Promoting the bat to DH is not automatically easier, with Herrera already receiving substantial DH work.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports misses against outer-half breaking balls and a popup-heavy pull/lift pattern, despite encouraging receiving foundations.
players.checkpoint: Make more contact with breaking balls away, reduce popups and sustain receiving quality through a larger workload.
players.monitor: Watch outside-breaking-ball contact and popup rates at advanced levels; avoid assuming every strikeout has the same cause.
players.need: Catching offense has room to improve on Pagés’ .587 OPS and Crooks’ .591, but Bernal and Herrera are also in the queue; defense remains essential.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Eli Willits
players.why: A brief Double-A appearance is enough to keep the fast-mover route visible, not enough to establish readiness. Washington has Abrams at short, but second-base production presents a possible area for improvement.
players.opportunity: An Abrams-to-second reshuffle could create a shortstop route; that is our scenario, not a confirmed club plan. Willits first needs to show he can handle advanced pitching over a meaningful sample.
players.observed: FanGraphs’ April report describes excellent contact/defensive potential but missing present power and late contact that limited pulled fastballs.
players.checkpoint: Get on time to pull firm fastballs and add extra-base impact without sacrificing contact or shortstop defense.
players.monitor: Watch pulled fastball damage against higher-level velocity. A tiny Double-A sample cannot resolve whether his bat is ready.
players.need: Second-base offense is a potential need: Nuñez posted a .535 OPS and Vivas .653. Moving Abrams is one possible response, not an announced decision.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Aidan Miller
players.why: The older scouting record supports an advanced infield bat, but the saved 2026 record has just 14 total PA, only 11 in Double-A. That cannot establish current readiness or explain the missing workload.
players.need: Bohm’s .698 OPS leaves room for a possible third-base upgrade; Turner logged 154 games at short. No injury or vacancy is being assumed.
players.opportunity: First establish current health and a sustained workload, then demonstrate usable defense at second or third rather than relying on a shortstop label.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports vulnerability to breaking balls away and inconsistent hands/throwing accuracy, with second or third possible alternatives behind Turner.
players.checkpoint: Handle sliders on the outer third, make accurate routine throws and demonstrate a sustained return to game action.
players.monitor: Verify the reason for the thin 2026 sample and current availability before raising the arrival outlook; no diagnosis is inferred.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Jarlin Susana
players.role: Power pitching: starter or shorter role
players.why: Advanced-level exposure keeps a 2027 debut possible, but the saved Triple-A sample is only 2.2 innings and the entire season just 20.1. That is a workload question before it is a ranking question.
players.need: Irvin posted a 5.48 ERA and other depth options also struggled, giving Washington a reason to look for better innings. A job still has to be earned.
players.opportunity: Prove he is available for sustained work, then compete for rotation innings. A shorter relief assignment could arrive before a full starting role.
players.observed: FanGraphs documents prior elbow/lat interruptions and an inconsistent, rarely used changeup behind the fastball/slider combination.
players.checkpoint: Sustain healthy outings and land a usable third pitch without letting the changeup sail out of the hand.
players.monitor: Verify current health, workload and changeup execution; historical injury reporting does not establish present clearance.
players.organization: Yoho and a Bottle of Rum
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Jaxon Wiggins
players.role: Power arm: relief could precede starts
players.why: The Triple-A label puts him close geographically, but the saved walk rate and limited workload argue against calling him ready from proximity alone.
players.need: Cabrera posted a 5.96 ERA and Rea 4.34, so improved pitching depth would help. Chicago still has several competing MLB starting options.
players.opportunity: A healthy, strike-throwing multi-inning role could be the first route. Regular starts require a stronger workload and command case than the saved season supplies.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports recurrent elbow interruptions and below-average command, especially inconsistent breaking-ball feel, despite a powerful fastball.
players.checkpoint: Demonstrate healthy repeat outings and land breakers consistently; lower walks before asking for a regular starting job.
players.monitor: Confirm current availability separately from the May report, then track breaking-ball strikes and walks per batter.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Kemp Alderman
players.why: A full Triple-A sample gives his power a realistic depth route, but a high strikeout rate keeps this from being a straightforward readiness endorsement.
players.need: Miami already has Hernández in left, Caissie/Conine in right and Stowers moving across corners. A part-time power need is more plausible than a vacant everyday position.
players.opportunity: Out-hit a bench or corner option, possibly in a matchup role. Merely moving to DH does not avoid competition from other bat-first players.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports chase and misses against spin low/away, plus late contact against fastballs, despite exceptional raw impact.
players.checkpoint: Lay off breaking balls below and away and get on time against fastballs without losing damage.
players.monitor: Track chase on spin and fastball timing separately; home-run totals cannot establish whether either problem improved.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.

players.name: Brandon Clarke
players.why: Only four saved Double-A innings make this an accelerated-path case rather than a near-ready starter claim. The arm could fit a shorter role before it supports a full rotation workload.
players.need: Liberatore’s 5.23 ERA leaves performance pressure in the rotation, but several alternatives already have substantial starts. Clarke also competes with Doyle for future innings.
players.opportunity: Demonstrate availability and reliable strikes before a bullpen or depth opportunity becomes actionable. Do not assume the club will shorten his development simply to fill a need.
players.observed: FanGraphs documents repeated health interruptions and erratic fastball control, with a slider more consistently located than the heater.
players.checkpoint: Repeat healthy outings and locate the fastball without walks, hit batters or wild misses overwhelming the slider.
players.monitor: Verify current clearance and delivery consistency; a four-inning Double-A sample cannot establish a new command level.
players.etaContext: Saved league profile label; not an independently calibrated debut forecast.
